## 2026-10-10 — a fleet companion tried on the default: its start refused the same on both transports, and one read of an online pilot found and stopped

Commit `6b99d53`, pushed. Next's head: what was not measured before the default changed, the
fleet's companions first.

**What was tried.** A companion run on the BFF's own host, started as the page starts one
(the page's setup, its grant and its route, from a script): Test Pilot forms a fleet and
invites Test Three, both docked at Jita; Test Three accepts from its own session; that
session then asks the host to fly it as a companion. On the default BFF (the game port),
then on the one told `gateway`, the store put back between.

**What came of it.**

- **The start was refused on both, with the same words**: 502, "Join a fleet first — a
  companion takes its orders from one." The pilot's own read a second earlier named the
  fleet it had joined. So nothing of the companion's ladder ran on either transport, and the
  two were not compared beyond that.
- **Read, not measured:** the start lets the caller's session go and the host chooses the
  pilot again for itself; the server takes a member out of its fleet when its session ends
  (`fleetRuntime.js`, `handleSessionDisconnected`); and the host's own check that the pilot
  is in a fleet is made after. I did not watch the member leave, so I do not say that is
  why.
- **The page has no way to post a fleet's advert** (nothing in `web/src` calls the advert
  routes), and no recording has one posted. The companions window joins a fleet by its
  advert's name, so its run of 2026-09-13 had an advert from somewhere else.

**One thing the tally showed, mended.** On the default BFF the run left one row the cutover
wants empty: a read of the web gateway's snapshot for a pilot who was online on this BFF.
It was the start route's check that the pilot is the caller's, made while the caller's own
session held that pilot. A pilot a web session holds was shown to be the account's when it
was chosen, by that same read; the route now takes that, and asks only about a pilot the
caller does not hold (`/api/bots/start` in `src/server.js`).

**Proof.**

- 1 new test, on the real routes and the real host: a start by the session holding the
  pilot asks once less; a start with nobody holding it, with another session holding it, and
  for a character that is not the account's each ask as before, and the last is still
  refused. Seen to fail on the commit before.
- 4 ways of breaking it were tried; all caught.
- Suite: 10094 tests, 10070 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **Live, on the default BFF, the same run again:** the tally's "online" class had one row
  before and none after. Nothing of a pilot's, nothing unheld and nothing unlisted either
  time.
- The store was put back after each run (the same as the copy), and the copies deleted.

**Not done, and why.**

- **The companion itself was not seen flying on the game port.** A server run could not be
  started (above), and a run in the tab wants an advertised fleet, which I had no made way
  to post.
- **The same ownership read at eight other places** (`store.getCharacterForAccount` in
  `src/server.js`: the select, two structure access checks, the customs haul's plan, a
  provisioning check and three fleet checks of each member). Each asks the gateway for one
  character's snapshot whether or not that pilot is online here. Only the bot start's was
  seen in a tally. The account's own list of characters would answer the same question
  without naming an online pilot.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **I did not change how a companion starts.** Whether a server run should be startable for
  a pilot the tab has just put in a fleet is a question of how the feature is meant to
  work, and it is the same on the gateway. It is listed, with what was read.

**For the operator.** If a server-run companion did start for you before with its pilot in
a fleet, how the pilot came to be in that fleet in the host's own session is the thing I
could not find; one line on that would save a lot of reading.

## 2026-10-10 — the training reads on the default: the same answers on both transports, and a flown pilot's skills no longer asked of the gateway

Commit `19cb173`, pushed. Next's head: what was not measured before the default changed, the
Factory and the training flows.

**What the Factory and the training flows ask, read first.**

- Pilot Training's reads (`/api/pilot-training/*`, `/api/roster/training`) are the account's:
  the account's list of characters, a pilot's skill sheet, the corporation's fittings and
  registry asked as a pilot who is not logged in (which the plan's 2.3 names).
- The training queue's review and apply refuse a pilot who is online
  (`PILOT_MUST_BE_OFFLINE`), so what they ask the gateway is of an offline pilot by rule.
- The Factory takes a pilot's session for itself in one flow only, the corporation
  onboarding (a trainee and a director chosen together, `factorySessions.withSessions`), and
  that chooses through the seam, so on the default it is a game-port session. Its skill
  purchase is refused outright as having no stock equivalent.

**What was measured.** Five training reads of account `test2` through each BFF, first with
nobody flying Test Two and then with Test Two chosen in another web session of the same BFF
(`training-walk.js`).

- Every read answered 200 on both BFFs, and each answer was the same on the default BFF as
  on the one told `gateway`, in both halves (but for who holds the pilot, which both said
  alike).
- **The tally of the default BFF had one row the cutover wants empty:** the gateway's
  `skills` asked for Test Two while Test Two was online on that BFF. It was Pilot Training's
  read of the pilot.

**What was built.** A read the account makes of a pilot's skills (`accountSkillSheet` in
`src/server.js`): for a pilot of that account that is online on this BFF on the game port,
the sheet is made from the pilot's own session, as its Skills window has it; the gateway is
asked for a pilot nobody here is flying, for one held through the gateway, and when the
session cannot say. The hangar's roster of who is training what, the roster's planetary
board (for a pilot's skills), Pilot Training's two reads and mining preparation now ask
that way. The training read itself takes "whom to ask" from its caller
(`src/pilotTrainingRead.js`), and asks the gateway when told nothing.

**Proof.**

- 2 new tests. The roster's read of two pilots, one flown on the game port: the flown one's
  from its session, the other's from the gateway, the gateway's again when the session
  fails (and the web session that flies the pilot still holds it), a pilot flown through the
  gateway read from the gateway, and **another account asking of the flown pilot never
  answered from the session**. And the training read asking whoever it is told. Both seen
  to fail on the commit before.
- 10 ways of breaking it were tried; all caught.
- Suite: 10096 tests, 10072 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **Live, the walk again on the changed default BFF:** Pilot Training's read of Test Two had
  the same digest with nobody flying it (the gateway's sheet) as with it flown (its own
  session's), the same as before the change and as through the gateway BFF; and the tally
  had no read of an online pilot's skills. The roster's training rows for a flown pilot and
  an unflown one were the same through each BFF.
- The store was put back after each run that chose a pilot, and the copy deleted.

**Measured, not mended.**

- **The roster's planetary board still reads the gateway's snapshot of a pilot who is
  online here** (`/api/roster/planets`: one such row in the tally, with Test Two flown). On
  the game port the pilot's own planets read has its colonies; the board does not use it.
- **Two of the five call sites changed have no test of their own and were not seen live**:
  mining preparation's read of a pilot's skills, and Pilot Training's qualification read.
  They ask through the same function as the three that were.

**Not seen.**

- The corporation onboarding (the one Factory flow that takes sessions): it wants a player
  corporation with a director on a second account, which this store has not got.
- The training queue applied: it wants a plan as the page builds one, which the walk did
  not build.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **A pilot flown through the gateway is still read from the gateway.** The change is for
  the game port only; the other transport is the way back and stays as it was.
- **When the pilot's session cannot make a sheet, the gateway is asked** rather than the
  read failing, and the session is left alone: a roster's read is not the pilot's own, and
  should not be what drops a pilot.

## 2026-10-10 — an ice site and an ore anomaly on both transports: the same things, the same rocks, and other words for a site's furniture

Commit `c82dfa7`, pushed. Next's head: what was not measured before the default changed, a gas
cloud's row. No gas site was found to look at; an ice site and an ore anomaly were, and
those two had not been measured either.

**What I had read, and what the rows said.** Reading the server, I took an ice chunk to be
called "iceChunk" by the gateway and to carry none of a rock's mining fields, which would
have made my own rock mend of this morning a new difference (the game port calling ice a
rock where the gateway did not). I did not write that down as found. The rows say
otherwise: through the gateway an ice chunk is "asteroid", with what it yields.

**What was measured.** Test Two undocked, moved to Halaima by the GM console, the scanner's
sites read, and a warp made to the ice site (archetype 28) and then to an ore anomaly (27).
Through the gateway BFF, then on the default BFF (the game port), the store put back
between.

- **The same number of rows on each grid** (94 at the ice site, 163 at the anomaly).
- **The rocks the same field for field but one.** 19 chunks of White Glaze at the ice
  site, and 73 rocks of six ores at the anomaly: each "asteroid", yielding its own type, of
  no belt, with the BFF's own grade and family ("ice" or "ore") beside. The one field that
  differs is what is left in a rock: a number through the gateway, nothing on the game
  port, as was known (a client is not told).
- **A site's furniture has other words.**

  | thing | gateway | game port |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | the ice field's anchor (type 17774, the asteroid belt's group) | "iceFieldAnchor" | "asteroidBelt" |
  | a site's objective marker at the ice field (the same type) | "siteObjectiveMarker" | "asteroidBelt" |
  | an anomaly's marker (group 885) | "universeAnomalySite", "siteObjectiveMarker" | "celestial" |
  | a site's scenery (groups 226 and 227) | "siteEnvironmentProp" | "celestial" |

  The gateway's are the server's own names for what it placed. A client has the slim item's
  category and group. Nothing in the page reads any of the gateway's four by name: its
  mining finds a belt by its group, which is the same on both.

**What was built.** Nothing in the source. One test pins what the game port calls these
things, from the rows' own types and groups, and two ways of breaking it were caught.
Suite: 10097 tests, 10073 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.

**Not seen.**

- **A gas cloud.** The server's generator gives ice sites only in the 280 systems I asked
  it about (40 of them have one); gas sites are the dungeon service's, behind a signature
  that wants probing. By the projection as it stands a gas cloud (group 711, a celestial's
  category) would be a "celestial" with none of a rock's fields on the game port. What the
  gateway says of one I do not know, and after this morning's wrong reading of ice I will
  not guess.
- **A bot mining ice on the game port.** The rows are the same as the gateway's but for
  what is left; no ice harvester was fitted and run.
- **In the browser.** The rows were read by script through each BFF, not on the page.

**Measured in passing.**

- **The tactical view draws a thing of a kind it does not know as a ship** (`bracketRole`
  falls through to "ship"), so the gateway's four site kinds are ships there, and on the
  game port the same things are celestials or belts. I did not look at either on the page.

**A slip, caught.** A walk script of mine lost its backslashes on the way through a shell
(a regular expression that then matched nothing, and read as "no sites"). The brief already
says to write such things with the Write tool; I had piped a patch through the shell
instead. The run that said "no sites" was not believed because the same answer's first
500 characters, printed beside it, had a site in them.

## 2026-10-10 — whose a character is, asked of the account's own list: nine reads of a character's snapshot gone

Commit `18e4db3`, pushed. Next's head: the ownership read at eight more call sites, answered
so that it never names a pilot who is online here.

**What it was.** `store.getCharacterForAccount` is asked in nine places of `src/server.js`:
a pilot's choosing, a bot's start, two structure access checks, the customs haul's plan, a
provisioning check and the fleet's three parking and delivery checks. It read the web
gateway's snapshot of the one character and took that character's row out of it, whoever
was flying the pilot. An earlier mend of today's (`6b99d53`) took one of the nine out of the
way for a pilot the caller holds; the other eight still named an online pilot whenever one was asked about.

**Measured before building.** For each of this server's eight characters, the row that read
gives was set beside the same character's entry in the account's own list of characters
(the gateway's `characters`, which the plan keeps as account-level): the same, field for
field, and the server's own record under it with the same keys. Pilot Training's code
already asked the list for the same question, and says why.

**What was built.** `getCharacterForAccount` in `src/eveStore.js` answers from the account's
own list. All nine call sites are served by it; none was changed.

**What changes for a caller.** Only what is heard of a character that is not the account's.
The snapshot's read threw the gateway's refusal (403, `CHARACTER_ACCOUNT_MISMATCH`), which
went through each route unchanged. The list simply has no such character, so the answer is
null and each route says its own refusal, as each was written to:

| asked of somebody else's pilot | before | now |
| --- | --- | --- |
| choosing it | 403 `CHARACTER_ACCOUNT_MISMATCH` | 404 `CHARACTER_NOT_FOUND` |
| a bot's start for it | 403 `CHARACTER_ACCOUNT_MISMATCH` | 404 `CHARACTER_NOT_FOUND` |
| a structure search for it | 403 `CHARACTER_ACCOUNT_MISMATCH` | 403 `STRUCTURE_PILOT_UNAVAILABLE` |

Nothing in the page or the BFF reads the gateway's code by name.

**Proof.**

- 6 new tests of the store's own function, the gateway client stood in for: the account's
  character, one it has not got, a row of another account's in the list, no ids, the
  gateway's refusal heard, and a snapshot handed in. Four seen to fail before the change
  (the other two say what did not change).
- 8 ways of breaking it were tried; all caught.
- Suite: 10103 tests, 10079 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **Against the real gateway:** the eight characters again, each the same as before; a
  character not the account's is null.
- **Live, on the default BFF on the change, beside the other BFF on the code before:** with
  Test Two flown in one web session, another session of the account asked a structure
  search and a bot's start for it. The answers were the same on both. The tally of the BFF
  on the code before had two reads of an online pilot's snapshot (and ten of an offline
  one's); the tally of the BFF on the change had no snapshot read at all.
- Six pilots of three accounts chosen on the changed BFF and logged out, yours among them.
- The store was put back after each run that chose a pilot, and the copy deleted.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **Somebody else's pilot is "not found" to a choosing, where it was "not yours".** It no
  longer says that the character exists under another account. I think that is the better
  answer; it is a change in what an API caller hears, and is in the table above.

**What is left of the snapshot.** The roster's planetary board and stock, and the customs
haul's plan: a pilot's colonies and goods out of the store. Of a pilot who is online here
that is still a read the cutover wants gone; the colonies can come from the pilot's own
session on the game port, the goods everywhere it owns cannot yet.

## 2026-10-10 — the brief's whole run, in the browser, on the game port, twice from a cold start

No commit of code: nothing needed mending. The roster's planetary board was Next's head; I
looked at it, left it with a question for the operator (below), and did what nobody had yet
done: the run the brief's fifth "done" line names.

**The run** (the brief, "When to stop", 5): log in, select a character, read inventory,
fitting, wallet, market, skills, mail and chat while docked; accept a courier mission;
undock; warp, jump a gate and dock by autopilot with the overview drawn from our own
ballpark; deliver and complete the mission; lock a target and cycle a module; log off.

**How it was run.** In the browser, on the check BFF that has nothing said about the
transport (so the game port), as Test Two. The server was started cold for each pass from
the same saved store, and the BFF restarted with it. One thing was staged before saving
that store: a 1MN Afterburner I fitted to Test Two's Badger, so that there was a module to
cycle. The courier offer was the pilot's own, already in its journal. Everything in the run
was done by pressing what is on the page.

**Pass 1 and pass 2, each:**

| step | what the page showed |
| --- | --- |
| log in, choose the pilot | docked at Muvolailen X - Moon 3 |
| inventory | the Badger, its hold (0.1 of 3,900 m³, one stack), an empty item hangar |
| fitting | Badger, the afterburner fitted and online |
| wallet | 9,999,207,418 ISK, with its recent activity |
| market | the groups of the market |
| skills | 385,914 skill points, 52 skills |
| mail | 15 unread, the inbox's rows |
| chat | Local of Muvolailen, with its messages |
| the courier mission | offered; the conversation opened, Accept pressed: accepted and active |
| the package, the route | "Load package into ship", then "Set autopilot to dropoff": the ship undocked by itself |
| autopilot | three jumps (Muvolailen, Annaro, Isutaka, Tasabeshi), each a warp to the gate and a jump, then a warp to the station and a docking, in about three minutes; the overview's rows changed with each grid (91, 80, 46, 134 and so on, none during a jump) |
| deliver and complete | "Complete Mission": completed, the journal empty, the wallet at 9,999,238,218 ISK (the reward 13,800 and the time bonus 17,000, both listed) |
| lock and cycle | undocked; the afterburner pressed and active; a sentry gun locked at 42 km (some twenty seconds of "Locking…"); the afterburner pressed off |
| dock and log off | docked from the overview; "Log out"; the page back with nobody in |

**What stood behind it, each pass.**

- The gateway's tally: nothing of a pilot's, nothing of an online pilot, nothing unheld,
  nothing unlisted. Account-level reads and one chat session only.
- The game port's ledger: 93 kinds of call, 252 calls, the same both times (164 and 165
  the same as the retail client's, 84 and 83 put into its shape by the transport, 4 not
  checked: the gate jumps and one more).
- The server's log: no packet error. The BFF's own log: no error or warning.

**So the brief's fifth line is met**, with the one staged module said. The other four are
not: the plan's Phase 5 has its removals to come and Phase 6 is not begun (lines 1 and 3),
and line 4 is the long list below.

**Measured in passing, not mended.**

- **Local's message of the day shows its markup** (`<b><color=0xfff4d35e>…</color></b><br>`
  as text).
- **A locked sentry gun shows no shield, armour or hull** (three dashes).
- **The package was in the hold before the mission was accepted** (one stack of Reports),
  and after the mission was completed the hold had that and an Encoded Data Chip. "Load
  package into ship" changed nothing I could see. Read on pass 1 only.
- **The BFF asked the gateway for the account 187 times in pass 1** (about ten minutes).
  It is account-level; it is also once for nearly every request the page makes.

**The roster's planetary board, looked at and left.** The board reads a pilot's colonies
and every planetary good it owns, wherever it sits, out of the gateway's snapshot. For a
pilot who is online here the colonies could come from its own session (the pilot's own
planets read does that on the game port). The goods cannot, as a client knows them: a
client is told a station's top-level items and nothing of what is inside a ship or a
container in a station it is not docked at. So there are two honest ways, and they are the
operator's to pick between:

- keep the snapshot for the boards whether the pilot is online or not, and say so in the
  plan (management needs more than the retail protocol sees, as its section 2.3 already
  says of offline pilots); or
- show an online pilot's board only what a client could know, which is less than it shows
  now.

I recommend the first, and have changed nothing.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **A module was staged for the run.** The brief's run wants one cycled, and Test Two's
  Badger had none. It is said above and was done before the store was saved.
- **The run was made by a script pressing the page's own buttons**, the pane being hidden.
  Nothing was sent that the page did not send for itself.

## 2026-10-10 — Phase 6 begun: one socket for a tab, carrying a route's operation in process

Commit `fa2f060`, pushed. Next's head: Phase 6a's first slice.

**What the plan asks** (Phase 6a): one WebSocket for a pilot carrying named operations, the
bodies of the existing routes unchanged, and the pushed notices; in place of the routes'
HTTP carriage, the event stream, and the cap of four requests the page keeps for itself.

**What was built** (`src/pilotSocket.js`, served by the BFF beside its routes).

- **The socket**, at `/api/socket`. A tab says hello with its web session's token, in a
  frame and never in the socket's address. Until it has, nothing is answered: no hello in
  ten seconds, or something else said first, and the socket is closed; a token that is
  nobody's, the same.
- **An operation is a route, run where it is.** A frame names a method and a path and may
  carry a body, with an id of the tab's choosing; the reply is that id with the route's own
  status and answer. The app is handed a request made in this process
  (`dispatchInProcess`), so a route's authentication, its checks, its body's limit and its
  errors are the route's own. Nothing of a route was rewritten, and every route the BFF has
  can be asked this way. It is also what a hosted bot wants in place of the loopback HTTP it
  makes today.
- Replies come as their routes finish, each by its id. The event stream and the socket's own
  path are not operations.
- **A server that is closing closes its sockets as the closing begins.** Found by a test that
  hung: an open socket is a connection, and a closing server waits for every connection to
  end.

**Not built yet, and so the routes and the event stream stand as they were:** the page does
not open the socket; the pushed notices are not carried on it; hosted bots still ask over
loopback.

**Two things found by the tests on the way.**

- **A request made in process had every body skipped.** The body parser asks whether a
  request is already finished before reading it, and takes one whose connection is not
  readable for finished. The stand-in for the connection said it was not. It is a stream of
  its own now and says it is, and the request says it is complete, or it is taken for one
  cut off once its body has been read.
- **A test that waits for a frame must not wait for ever.** The first run hung in the
  background until I stopped it; the waits are bounded now, so a socket that never answers
  fails its test.

**Proof.**

- 9 new tests. Each shape of route asked both ways, over HTTP and in process, and the
  answers set side by side: a read with a query, a write with a body, a route still at work
  after its body, one that throws, one that is no JSON, one with no answer, a body too big,
  a path nobody has. The hello and each way of failing it. An operation on the socket beside
  the same over HTTP. Two at once, the quick one answered first. Each frame that is no
  operation. And the BFF itself, started as it starts, with a route of its own asked both
  ways and its closing with a socket open. The BFF's own was seen to fail on the commit
  before.
- 23 ways of breaking it were tried, four of a file at a time. One survived at first (the
  socket letting go of the server's upgrades when closed, which nothing looked at); the test
  now counts the listeners, and all 23 are caught.
- Suite: 10112 tests, 10088 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **Live, a real socket to the default BFF**, from a store saved first: a hello with a token
  that is nobody's was closed (4401); with Test Two's account's, answered. Over the socket:
  the pilot chosen, then skills, wallet, fitting and journal each read and set beside the
  same read over HTTP, the same every time. The flight status differed, and differs the same
  way between two reads over HTTP: each read takes the notices waiting. Twenty-four reads
  asked at once on the one socket were all answered, in 14 ms. Logged out over the socket;
  the next operation was refused as it is over HTTP. The gateway's tally had nothing of a
  pilot's.
- The store was put back after, and the copy deleted. One more login and logout of the
  docked pilot was made afterwards, to see what differed in the flight status; nothing was
  staged for it.

**Measured in passing.**

- A path under `/api/` that no route has is answered 200 with the page itself, over HTTP and
  on the socket alike (the BFF's last route serves the page for any path).

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **The token goes in the first frame.** A browser cannot set a header on a WebSocket, and
  the address is the other place; the event stream puts it there and its route says what
  that costs. The cookie would also have come by itself, but the page signs each tab in on
  its own token, and a socket opened by a cookie could be opened by another site's page.
- **The socket carries any route, not one chosen operation.** "One named operation" was the
  slice I had written down. Carrying the route as it is made every route an operation at
  once, with nothing to choose.
- **No header of the tab's is passed to a route**, only the token's. The page sends no
  other today.

## 2026-10-10 — the page carries its requests on the tab's socket, behind a setting; and a socket's life

Commit `a69d228`, pushed. Next's head: Phase 6a, the page opens the socket.

**What was built.**

- **A fetch that goes by the socket** (`web/src/app/socketFetch.ts`). It has `fetch`'s own
  shape: a request is sent as an operation on the BFF's socket, and what comes back is a
  `Response`, so nothing that asks can tell which way it went. One socket for each token,
  since a tab can hold several pilots and a socket's hello names one session.
- **One place that says which way** (`web/src/app/pageFetch.ts`), asked by the page's three
  fetch sites (`requestJson`, `callMethod`, the fleet's fenced fetch). It is HTTP unless this
  browser's local storage has `evejs-web-transport:v1` set to `socket`. In Node, where the
  hosted bots run the same code, it is always the world's fetch.
- **HTTP is the way back, always.** Fetched as before: what has no token (a request that
  rides the cookie, the login itself), what is not the BFF's API, the event stream, a body
  that is not JSON; everything while a socket is down or was refused; and whatever the BFF
  says it did not run. A request sent and not answered when its socket closes fails, as a
  fetch cut off does, and is not asked again by any other way: it may have been run.

**A fault the browser found, and what was done.** With the setting on, a login with the
windows open worked, and had ten sockets open after a quarter of a minute. The hangar signs
in for one question and out again, account after account, and each of those sessions had
been given a socket that nothing closed. So a socket is for a session that stays:

- a token's first two requests go over HTTP, and it is given a socket at its third (a
  session made for one question asks it and logs out: two);
- its socket is closed when the session is logged out on it;
- one that nothing has been asked on for two minutes is closed when something else is
  asked.

**Proof.**

- 19 new tests (15 of the fetch, 4 of the setting): a request carried and answered by id,
  what cannot be carried, a socket for each token, a socket that never opens, a token
  refused, a request cut off, the BFF's "not run", a request given up on at each moment, a
  reply as a response, the third request, the logout, the idle one, and a replaced socket
  speaking late.
- 57 ways of breaking it were tried, four of a file at a time; three survived at first and
  were each settled: a clause that could not matter was taken out, a guard that could not
  matter was taken out, and the guards against a replaced socket were given a test that
  needs them. All that are left are caught.
- Suite: 10131 tests, 10107 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **In the browser, on the default BFF (the game port), the same login twice**, Test Two
  chosen with 25 windows open:

  | | setting not set (HTTP) | set to `socket` |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | requests to the BFF's API over HTTP | 128 | 45: the logins, each session's first two, and what has no token |
  | frames sent on sockets | 0 | 92, of 38 different operations |
  | sockets open | 0 | 3 (before the fault was mended: 10) |
  | the page | docked, wallet, skills, chat, journal | the same |

- **A write, with the setting on:** Undock and Dock pressed on the page. Both went as frames
  (`/api/bridge/flight/undock`, `/api/bridge/flight/dock`), the overview had its 91 rows in
  space, and in that time no request of the bridge's went over HTTP (112 frames). The pilot
  was logged out with the page's button, and its socket was closed by the page.
- The gateway's tally through all of it: nothing of a pilot's. The BFF's log: no error.
- The setting was taken off again and the page left with nobody in. The store was put back
  and the copy deleted.

**Not done.**

- **The cap of four** (`MAX_IN_FLIGHT` in `web/src/app/transport.ts`) still holds for what
  goes on the socket. It is there for the browser's six connections, which a socket does not
  use; lifting it for what is carried is the next small thing.
- **The pushes** are still the event stream's.
- **The three sites' asking has no test of its own**: in Node the answer is always the
  world's fetch. It is what the browser's run shows.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **It is off unless set.** The routes and the event stream are what the page uses by
  default, as before. To try it: in the browser's console,
  `localStorage.setItem("evejs-web-transport:v1", "socket")` and reload; `removeItem` to go
  back.
- **A token's third request, not its first.** It costs a staying session two requests over
  HTTP, and saves a handshake for every session that is made for one question.
- **A request cut off is not retried over HTTP**, even a read. A read could be, but a
  request's method does not say which it is here: many of the BFF's reads are POSTs (the
  generic call, the names). So nothing is retried.

## 2026-10-10 — a request carried on the tab's socket waits for no lane

Commit `ab125f2`, pushed. Next's head: Phase 6a, the cap of four lifted for what is carried.

Nothing of the retail client's is in this unit: the cap is the page's own, there because a
browser has six connections to an origin (`web/src/app/transport.ts`).

**What was built.**

- **The lane can be told a request is carried** (`bridgeLane.run(priority, path, task,
  { carried: true })`). Such a request is started in the tick it is asked, holds no lane and
  waits behind nothing; it is counted (`carried()`), and still has its own deadline, set in
  the task. Everything not said to be carried takes its turn as before.
- **The socket's fetch says whether it would carry a request now** (`wouldCarry`,
  `web/src/app/socketFetch.ts`): only what can be an operation, and only on that token's
  socket once the hello is answered. Asking sends nothing, opens nothing and is not counted
  towards a token's third request.
- **The page's two fetch sites ask, and tell the lane** (`requestJson` in
  `web/src/app/api.ts`, `callMethod` in `web/src/bridge/callMethod.ts`, by way of
  `pageCarries` in `web/src/app/pageFetch.ts`).

**What still takes a lane, and why.**

- A request that goes over HTTP: all of them with the setting off, and with it on the
  logins, a session's first two, and what has no token.
- A request asked while its socket is being made. If the socket never opens it falls to
  HTTP, which needs a connection.
- A request made with a fetch handed in: a hosted bot's, and the fleet's one fenced
  invitation (`web/src/app/flow.ts`), which goes on the socket and keeps its turn.

**Proof.**

- 4 new tests, and a line added to a fifth: two of the lane (eight carried at once with
  both lanes held and one waiting; a carried one that cannot be started), one of
  `wouldCarry` at each moment of a socket's life, and one that stands a page up in Node (a
  `location`, the setting in a storage, a `WebSocket` and a `fetch` answered by hand) and
  makes requests with the page's own two fetch sites on the page's one lane. That last one
  is also the first test of the two sites' asking for the socket's fetch at all, which the
  entry before this said had none.
- 19 ways of breaking it were tried, four of a file at a time; all are caught. One clause
  was taken out before the pass because nothing could tell it was there (`pageCarries`
  asking for a `location`: the socket's fetch is only ever made where there is one).
- With the sources of the commit before, five fail (the four new tests, and the setting's
  file, which cannot import what is not there yet); with these, all 39 pass.
- Suite: 10135 tests, 10111 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **In the browser, on the default BFF (the game port):** the page reloaded, Test Two's row
  clicked in the hangar, and everything the page asked of `/api/` counted from that click
  until 2.5 s had passed with nothing outstanding (the probe is `login-probe.js` in the
  scratchpad):

  | | setting not set (HTTP) | `socket`, the cap held (`a69d228`) | `socket`, the cap lifted (`ab125f2`) |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | runs | 4 | 1 | 3 |
  | requests over HTTP | 69 | 6 | 6 |
  | frames sent | 0 | 63 | 63, 63, 62 |
  | most outstanding at once | 5 | 5 | 32 |
  | click to the last answer | 540, 797, 525, 612 ms | 587 ms | 479, 521, 488 ms |
  | windows with something in them | 25 | 25 | 25 |

  What the table says and no more: the number outstanding at once went from 5 to 32, and
  the same windows were filled. The times are close and their spreads all but touch (521
  against 525); on this machine, with the BFF and the server on loopback, the cap cost
  little. The first HTTP run was on the build before, the other three on this one; the
  capped socket was run once and cannot be run again without building the commit before.
  The 5 where the cap is four is the probe counting every fetch of `/api/`, in the lane or
  not; which one is outside it was not looked for.
- The BFF's log through the runs: no error. The gateway's tally: nothing of a pilot's
  (pilot 0, online 0, unlisted 0, unheld 0). The last 400 requests the tab made of the BFF
  all answered 200. The tab's console does hold older lines saying 502, from before those
  400; when they were made was not found (the server is stopped for the store's copy
  while the page is open and asking, which was not checked as their cause).
- The setting was taken off, the pilot logged out with the page's button, the page left
  with nobody in ("In client 0"), and the viewport put back. The store was put back and the
  copy deleted; both check BFFs were restarted on the committed code.

**Slips of mine, and what they cost.**

- The first test of `wouldCarry` left a request unanswered when it ended, and Node said so
  ("asynchronous activity after the test ended"). It was rewritten on the file's own rig
  with every request answered.
- I converted a list of breakages to CRLF because `file` said the source had CRLF endings.
  The tool matches on LF whatever the file has, so three of the breakages were not tried.
  They were run again as they should be written, and caught.

**Not done.**

- **The pushes** are still the event stream's. Next.
- **The fleet's fenced invitation** has no test of its going on the socket.
- **A cap of the socket's own.** There is none: whatever the page asks at once is sent at
  once, and the BFF runs each as it arrives. 32 at once were seen answered. Whether the BFF
  should bound what one socket has running is a question for the slice that takes the HTTP
  carriage away.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **A request asked while the socket is being made keeps a lane.** It costs a staying
  session's third request a turn in the queue, and means a socket that never opens cannot
  put more than four requests on the browser's connections.
- **A fetch handed in is never carried**, whatever the page is set to.
- **The setting is still off unless set.**

## 2026-10-10 — a pilot's pushed notices come on the tab's socket

Commit `7d85247`, pushed. Next's head: Phase 6a, the pushed notices on the socket in place of
the event stream.

Nothing of the game's protocol is in this unit: it is the page's hop to the BFF. (A retail
client is pushed its notices on the one connection its calls go on, which is where this
puts the page's.)

**What was built.**

- **The event stream, run where it is** (`streamInProcess`, `src/pilotSocket.js`). The BFF's
  event stream (`GET /api/bridge/events`, Server-Sent Events) is a route like the rest,
  except that it answers for as long as it is listened to. Asked for on the socket it is
  run in this process, like an operation, and each frame it writes is handed on as it is
  written. So who may listen, what is refused, the one gateway stream a held pilot has
  however many listen, and every frame are the route's own; `src/server.js` is not changed.

      browser -> BFF   { "events": "open", "n": 3 }
      BFF -> browser   { "events": { "open": true, "n": 3 } }
      BFF -> browser   { "event": { ...a frame of the event stream... } }
      BFF -> browser   { "events": { "ended": true, "n": 3, "status": 409, "body": { ... } } }
      browser -> BFF   { "events": "close" }

  A socket has one event stream; asked for again, the one attached is let go and another
  attached. `n` is the page's to choose and is said back, so that what is said of a stream
  the page has let go is not taken for the one it has now. A socket that closes takes its
  stream with it.
- **The page listens there** (`listen` in `web/src/app/socketFetch.ts`; `subscribeBridgeEvents`
  in `web/src/app/api.ts`). Where the page is set to the socket, a pilot's live channel is
  its socket and no `EventSource` is opened. A session that is listened to is one that
  stays, so it is given its socket then, whatever it has asked so far; and a socket being
  listened on is not closed for having had nothing asked on it.
- **The `EventSource` is the way back.** It is opened in the socket's place if the socket
  cannot be made, never opens, is refused, goes down while listened on, or cannot carry
  the asking. A socket let go on purpose (a logout, the page closing them) sends its
  listener nowhere.

**Where it knowingly differs from an `EventSource`.**

- An `EventSource` asks again by itself a few seconds after its stream ends. A listener on
  the socket is told once that the BFF ended or refused the stream, and is not asked for
  again. The page listens anew each time a pilot is chosen (`startLiveStream`), which is
  when a stream that ended has something to come back to.
- The event stream's heartbeat (a comment every 25 s, for what stands between) is not
  handed on. Nothing on the socket takes its place; a page with a pilot in asks things on
  it all the time.

**Proof.**

- 14 new tests. Eight of the BFF's end (`test/pilotSocketEvents.test.js`): the stream run in
  process (its status once, each thing as written, its closing, a refusal, an ending, no
  route, something thrown), the frames in what a stream writes, the frames on a socket
  beside its operations, a stream let go three ways, a stream refused and ended and asked
  for again, what is no asking; and the BFF's own route with a gateway whose pushes the
  test makes, listened to on the socket and over HTTP side by side: the same frames, one
  gateway stream for both, kept while either listens, resumed from where it had got to.
  Five of the page's socket (`socketFetch.test.ts`) and one of the page stood up in Node
  with its own `subscribeBridgeEvents` (`pageCarried.test.ts`).
- 68 ways of breaking it were tried, four of a file at a time. Five survived at first.
  Three were guards nothing could tell were there, and were taken out (a token that is a
  string and not empty; an error handed on after a stream was over; the way back not taken
  by a listener that has stopped, which cannot be asked of one). Two were given tests (a
  frame about the stream that says neither thing; a refusal that looks like a frame). All
  that are left are caught. Four more statements were taken out while the list was being
  written, for the same reason.
- With the sources of the commit before, all 14 fail; with these, they pass.
- Suite: 10149 tests, 10125 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **In the browser, on the default BFF (the game port), the same flight three times**: Test
  Two chosen from the hangar, an undock, a quarter of a minute in space, a docking, a
  logout. A probe in the page (`push-probe.js` in the scratchpad) counted the frames of the
  event stream by kind as they came on a socket and by an `EventSource`, and each
  `EventSource` made.

  | | setting not set | set to `socket` | set to `socket`, and the pilot's socket closed under the page after the login |
  | --- | --- | --- | --- |
  | `EventSource`s made | 1 | 0 | 1, when the socket closed |
  | asked for on a socket | never | once (`{"events":"open","n":1}`) | once; not again on the session's next socket |
  | frames by the `EventSource` | all | none | all after the close |
  | frames on the socket | none | all | those before the close |
  | the stream's status frames | connecting 1, live 1 | the same | connecting 2, live 2 (once each way) |
  | `snapshot` | 1 | 1 | 1 (none on the way back: the stream went on from where it was) |
  | `OnMachoObjectDisconnect` | 29 | 29 | 29 |
  | `OnModuleAttributeChanges` | 14 | 14 | 7 and then 7 |
  | `OnServerBrainUpdated` | 6 | 6 | 3 and then 3 |
  | `OnSessionChanged`, `OnItemsChanged` | 2 each | 2 each | 2 each |
  | `DoSimClockRebase`, `OnSetTimeDilation`, `OnMultiEvent`, `OnInvulunOnUndockingUpdated`, `OnInvulnCancelled`, `OnDockingAccepted`, `OnDockingFinished` | 1 each | 1 each | 1 each |
  | at the logout | status `ended` twice, then the `EventSource`'s error | status `ended` twice, then `{"events":{"ended":true,"status":200}}` | as the first column |
  | the page | in space with 91 rows, then docked | the same | the same |

  The same kinds in the same numbers each way, and with the socket closed under it nothing
  was told twice and nothing was missed.
- The BFF's log: no error; a line for each stream going live and for each ending. The
  gateway's tally: nothing of a pilot's (pilot 0, online 0, unlisted 0, unheld 0).
- The setting was taken off, the page left with nobody in ("In client 0"), the viewport put
  back. The store was put back and the copy deleted; both check BFFs were restarted on the
  committed code.

**A slip of mine, and a tool mended for it.** I wrote one small patch with a shell heredoc,
against my own note, and it broke two strings across lines in the new test file. The file
then did not load, and the breakage tool, run next, called its breakage "caught": every
breakage is caught by a test file that fails before it starts. The next plain run of the
tests showed it; the strings were mended with a script written to a file, and the breakage
tried again and caught. `scripts/break-and-check.js` now runs the tests once before it
breaks anything and refuses to go on if they fail ("NOT TRIED any of N"), tried on a file
that loads and one that does not.

**Measured and not looked into.**

- **Status `ended` comes twice at a logout**, both ways. The BFF's log has "gateway refused
  the stream (404); session ended" at each logout: the pilot's stream is told the session
  is gone and then that it was released.
- **How often the page asks `/api/health`** with a live channel was not compared: with the
  setting on, that request goes on a socket, where the probe did not count it.

**Not done.**

- **A pilot in the background has no pushes**, either way. The page turns its live channel
  off because an `EventSource` holds one of the browser's connections for as long as it
  is open (`livePush`, `web/src/app/sessions.ts`). On a socket it holds none, so the reason
  is gone where the socket is open; giving every pilot in the tab its pushes there is a
  unit of its own, with what the page does with them for a pilot not on screen to be read
  first.
- **A question the server puts to the player** goes out on this stream, and waits for a
  listener. It was not put live in this unit: the frames are handed to the same function
  either way, which is what the tests hold.
- **A hosted bot's event stream** is still asked for over loopback HTTP
  (`src/hostedEventSource.js`). `streamInProcess` is what it wants; that is the next slice.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **The route is run in process, not given a second way out.** The stream's frames are
  written as Server-Sent Events by the route and read back into frames by the socket: a
  little work done twice, for a route left exactly as it is and one place that says who may
  listen. When the routes' HTTP carriage is taken away, the writing and the reading can go
  together.
- **The `EventSource` is the way back**, so a browser set to the socket that cannot have one
  still has its pushes. It holds a connection again while it is open.
- **It is still off unless set** (`evejs-web-transport:v1` = `socket` in local storage).

## 2026-10-10 — a hosted bot asks the BFF in the BFF's own process

Commit `f6327fa`, pushed. Next's head: Phase 6a, a hosted bot's requests made in process and
not over loopback.

Nothing of the game's protocol is in this unit: it is how the BFF's own bots reach the BFF.

**What was built.**

- **A fetch that asks the app where it is** (`src/inProcessFetch.js`). The hosted bots run the
  page's flows in the BFF's process, and those flows ask with `fetch`. They are now handed
  one that runs the request through the app in this process (`dispatchInProcess`) and
  answers with a `Response` made of what the route answered: its status, its headers, its
  body. No route and no flow is changed.
- **What is run in process:** a request to the BFF's own API at the BFF's own address, with
  a body that is text or absent. Anything else goes to the world's fetch as it was asked.
- **The event stream** is run with `streamInProcess` and answered with a body that is read
  as the route writes it, so the hosted event source (`src/hostedEventSource.js`) reads it
  as it read the loopback one, unchanged. Stopped, the route is told its listener has gone.
- **A request given up on** rejects with its signal's reason, as a fetch does. Its route is
  not stopped, as it is not stopped by a connection that closes.
- **The setting.** `EVEJS_HOSTED_BOT_REACH`: `inprocess` (the default) or `loopback`, which
  has the bots ask over HTTP as they did and is the way back. The compose file passes it
  on, the README names it, and the server says which it is as it starts.
- Two small additions under it in `src/pilotSocket.js`: a body sent as it is (`rawBody`),
  for a caller whose request is already written out; and a stream's headers said with its
  status, the ones handed straight to `writeHead` among them.

**What asking both ways found.**

- **One answer is not the same, and it is no route's.** A path no route has is answered 404
  both ways: over HTTP with the app's own last page ("Cannot GET ..."), in process with the
  refusal `dispatchInProcess` gives (`{ ok: false, error: "NOT_FOUND" }`), which is what the
  tab's socket says of it too. Left as it is, said in the module and tested as what it is.
  (In the BFF itself a read of an `/api/` path no route has is answered with the page, 200,
  both ways: that is in the list already.)
- **A request that would never have been answered.** Writing the list of breakages showed
  that an answer no `Response` can be made of (a status outside 200 to 599) threw where
  nobody was waiting, and left the asker waiting for ever. It is a fetch that failed now,
  for a request and for the stream's path, with a test of each.

**Proof.**

- 10 new tests. Eight of the fetch (`test/inProcessFetch.test.js`): fifteen shapes of request
  asked both ways of the same app and set side by side (the status, the content type, a
  header of the route's, a header said twice, every byte, and that the same route was
  reached); what goes elsewhere; a request given up on before and during; something thrown
  outside of every handler; a body sent as it is; the event stream read as it is written,
  stopped three ways and refused; the hosted event source reading it both ways and hearing
  the same; the setting. Two of the BFF itself with its real routes and its real bot host
  (`test/hostedStartOwnership.test.js`): in process, none of a hosted bot's requests comes
  in at the server's door, and its pilot is held; set to loopback, they come in there.
- That file's harness now tells the BFF its own address, as the BFF proper knows it, so
  all 47 of its tests make their hosted requests in process.
- 43 ways of breaking it were tried, four of a file at a time. Two survived: one changes
  nothing (a `Request` is no address of the API's whichever way it is read), and one was an
  upper-casing done twice, taken out. Two flags and a lower-casing were taken out before
  the pass, for the same reason.
- With the sources of the commit before, the in-process test fails and the fetch's own
  file does not load; with these, all pass.
- Suite: 10159 tests, 10135 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **Live, on the game port, the same bot run twice from the same store.** Test Two was given
  a Venture with two mining lasers through the BFF's own routes, and the store put aside as
  it then stood. The starter "Mine and haul cycle" was started by the page's own start and
  watched for 150 s, then stopped; the store was put back to the staged copy between the
  two runs. While each ran, the BFF's connections to itself were counted every five
  seconds (rows of `netstat` to the BFF's port owned by the BFF's own process).

  | | in process (the default) | `EVEJS_HOSTED_BOT_REACH=loopback` |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | the BFF's connections to itself | 0 in each of 38 samples | 5 or 6 in 33 of 39 samples; 2, 3, 4 and 7 once each; 0 in the first, before the bot had started, and in the last, after it was stopped |
  | Leaving the station | 2 s after the start | 2 s |
  | Flying to the belt | 4 s | 4 s |
  | In warp | 10 s | 10 s |
  | Approaching a rock | 22 s | 22 s |
  | Locking on | 34 s | 34 s |
  | Mining | 50 s | 50 s |
  | the bot's event stream | went live once | went live once |
  | the gateway's tally | nothing of a pilot's | nothing of a pilot's |
  | the BFF's error log | 1292 bytes | 1292 bytes: the usual warning, and one refusal (`TargetTooFar`, 409) |

  The watcher asks every two seconds, so the times are to two seconds.

**A slip of mine.** I read the size of the in-process run's error log and not what was in
it, and the restart for the second run wrote over it. The second run's is the same size to
the byte and holds one refusal by the server (a lock asked for on a rock out of reach). That
the first held the same is likely and was not read.

**Not done.**

- **How much was mined** each way was not compared.
- **A fleet's companions, a mining operation's pilots, two bots at once, and a bot brought
  back after a restart** were not run live in process. The first two are what the 47 tests
  run with real routes and a stand-in for the flows.
- **In a container** it was not run. Nothing of it knows where the BFF listens.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **In process is the default, and loopback the way back.** It is inside the BFF, both ways
  were seen to run the same bot the same, and a default that is off is never run. To go
  back: `EVEJS_HOSTED_BOT_REACH=loopback` in the BFF's environment. `.env.example` does not
  name it (I may not change that file); the README does.
- **The 404 for a path no route has is left as the socket has it.**

## 2026-10-10 — a socket's operations bounded; and the brief's whole run with the page on the socket, twice, set beside one over HTTP

Commit `c996cd6`, pushed. Next's head: the whole run with the page set to the socket, twice
from a cold start, and the bound settled, before the socket is made the page's default.

**The default was not turned.** The run passed both times on the socket. Set beside a pass
over HTTP it showed the same page and the same kinds of call, and more calls of two kinds.
That is to be found and mended first: it is the next unit.

**The bound** (`src/pilotSocket.js`). Over HTTP a tab could have the BFF doing four things
at once: the page's own cap, kept for the browser's connections. A socket has neither. So
a socket runs 32 operations at once (what a login was seen to ask for at once); one asked
past that waits its turn, in the order asked, up to 512 of them; and one asked past that is
answered at once with an error frame (`TOO_MANY`), which says it was not run and which the
page already takes as its word to ask over HTTP, where the old cap holds. What was waiting
is not run for a tab that has gone.

- 2 new tests, 13 ways of breaking it tried and all caught; with the source of the commit
  before, both fail. Suite: 10161 tests, 10137 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- The first run of one of the tests failed, rightly: the BFF's end of a socket's closing
  is done a moment after the tab's, and the test let a route finish in between. The test
  now waits for the BFF's end.

**The run.** As the entry of the first whole run has it: Test Two, an afterburner fitted to
its Badger beforehand, the courier offer its own; the server started cold from the same
saved store for each pass, and the BFF restarted with it; everything done by pressing what
is on the page. Two passes with `evejs-web-transport:v1` set to `socket`, then a third with
it not set, for the comparison. A probe in the page counted what went which way.

The two unanswered frames of each socket pass are what was out when the pilot logged out.

**The differences, as measured.**

- **Two kinds of call are made more often on the socket.** Call by call, the three ledgers
  differ in three rows: `dogmaIM.GetAllInfo` 21 and 23 on the socket against 15 over HTTP;
  `account.GetEntryTypes` 3 and 3 against 1; `invbroker.GetInventoryFromId` 11, 10 and 11.
  The first two are what the socket's passes have over the other. Of `GetAllInfo` I have
  read this much and proved none of it: the transport primes godma "once for a ship in a
  place" by a mark it sets when the answer is in (`shipReadings`, `src/gamePort/pilots.js`),
  so readers that come while the first is out would each ask, and more come together on the
  socket. Where `GetEntryTypes` is asked three times I have not found.
- **The refusals are the page's own, both ways.** Every 409 was the agent's window asking
  again of its own accord while the pilot docked or undocked, which the page does on
  purpose and tries again (`whenThePilotIsFree`, `web/src/app/flow.ts`): five or six at an
  undock, one to three at a docking. Over HTTP all 13 were `SESSION_CHANGE_IN_PROGRESS`; on
  the socket one at each undock was `CHARACTER_IN_USE` instead, which the page treats the
  same and which the BFF also writes to its error log.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **The bound's numbers.** 32 at once is what was seen to work for a login; 512 waiting is
  generous on purpose, so that the bound is only ever met by a page that has gone wrong.
- **The default waits.** A page that makes more calls of the server one way than the other
  is not yet "the same either way", and making it the default would put the difference in
  front of everyone. Found first, mended, and the three passes run again.
- **A third pass over HTTP was run** though the unit named two on the socket: the earlier
  HTTP run's ledger had been kept only as totals, and totals could not say which calls the
  nine more were.

## 2026-10-10 — what a client asks once is asked once however many ask together; and the socket made what the page uses

Commits `1ebaa67` (the two mends) and `bc9dbd3` (the default), pushed. Next's head: the page
on the socket made to ask of the server what it asks over HTTP, and then the default.

**What a retail client does** (the recordings first, then its code).

- **godma is primed at a change of place or ship, once.** `godma.py` 1154: at a session
  change that names `stationid`, `solarsystemid`, `shipid`, `charid` or `structureid` it
  primes itself, with `GetDogmaLM().GetAllInfo(primeCharacter, primeShip, primeStructure)`.
  On Tranquility ("Autopilot thru a few systems") two systems arrived at are two
  `GetAllInfo`, one each.
- **The names of a wallet entry's kinds are asked for once.** `accountsvc.py` 86,
  `GetStaticData`: kept in the service until the character changes. On Tranquility ("Open
  Wallet - Plex - Corp Wallet - Corp Transfers") `GetEntryTypes` was asked once while the
  wallet's transactions were asked three times.

**What was wrong.** Two of the transport's once-only askings were once only for askers that
came one after another (`src/gamePort/pilots.js`).

- `shipReadings` marked godma as primed when the answer was in. Each reader that came
  while the asking was out found it unmarked and asked again.
- `account.GetEntryTypes` went to the server each time the wallet was read, and was
  answered from the client's cache of method calls only once a first answer had been kept.

Over HTTP the page's cap of four hid most of it: 15 primings and 1 asking. On the tab's
socket, where a login asks thirty things at once, it was 21 and 23, and 3.

**Mended.** Whoever wants the ship's readings while godma's priming is out waits for the
one asking (and each is told the same where it fails: readings unknown, never the ones
from before). The account service's static data is kept as the client keeps it, by the
means the transport already has for a thing kept (`keptReads.js`), so that several that
want it together ask once.

- 4 new tests; 12 ways of breaking it tried. Two survived at first, both the same gap:
  nothing told "readings unknown" from "the old readings" where godma could not be primed
  again. A test was written that does, and both are caught. With the source of the commit
  before, all 4 fail.
- Suite: 10165 tests, 10141 pass, 0 fail, 0 cancelled, 24 skipped.

**The run again, three ways from the same cold start**: with the browser set to `socket`
(before the default was turned), with nothing set over HTTP as it then was, and, after the
default was turned and the page built again, with nothing set at all.

| | set to `socket` | over HTTP | nothing set, after the default was turned |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| the page | docked at Muvolailen with 25 windows, none empty; 9,999,207,418 ISK; the mission accepted; Muvolailen, Annaro, Isutaka, Tasabeshi and docked; completed, 9,999,238,218 ISK; the afterburner on, a sentry gun locked at 43 km, off; docked; logged out, nobody in | the same | the same |
| frames sent | 1526 | 0 | 1523 |
| `EventSource`s made | 0 | 1 | 0 |
| frames of the event stream | 357 | 356 | 357 |
| most outstanding at once | 35 | 5 | 37 |
| refused with 409, all the agent window's own asking again | 14 | 13 | 14 |
| the game port's ledger | 93 kinds, 249 calls | 93 kinds, 248 calls | 93 kinds, 248 calls |
| `dogmaIM.GetAllInfo` | 11 | 11 | 11 |
| `account.GetEntryTypes` | 1 | 1 | 1 |
| rows of the ledger that differ from the HTTP pass | one: the selection screen's data, 7 against 6 (I loaded the page twice for that pass, to set it) | | none |
| the gateway's tally | nothing of a pilot's | nothing of a pilot's | nothing of a pilot's |
| the server's log | no packet error | no packet error | no packet error |

So the page asks of the server on the socket what it asks over HTTP: the same calls, the
same number of each. (How many requests went over HTTP on the socket's passes is not in
the table: the probe began counting at a different moment of the hangar's sign-ins each
time.)

**The default** (`web/src/app/pageFetch.ts`). A pilot's requests and its pushed notices go
on its socket unless the browser is told otherwise. To tell one: in its console,
`localStorage.setItem("evejs-web-transport:v1", "http")`, and reload; `removeItem` to go
back. Seen in the browser on the same build: with `http` set, a login made no socket at
all (none was constructed), 97 requests over HTTP and one `EventSource`, and filled its 25
windows. The README says how.

**Measured and left.**

- **Eleven primings for eight places.** The run is in eight places (docked, four systems,
  docked, space, docked). The transport forgets its priming at any session change that
  names `stationid`, `structureid`, `solarsystemid`, `locationid` or `shipid`; the client's
  rule names `charid` and not `locationid`. Whether the three more are changes the client
  would prime at too is to be counted: the session's changes in the run, each with what it
  names. And the client primes the character once (`primeCharacter` false after the
  first, as on Tranquility: `(False, True, None)`), where the transport asks
  `(True, True, None)` every time.
- **`CHARACTER_IN_USE` in the BFF's error log**, twice a run on the socket and never over
  HTTP. It is the agent's window asking again while the pilot undocks, refused by one gate
  of the BFF's where over HTTP it meets another; the page takes both the same and tries
  again. The BFF's last handler writes every refusal that is thrown to that log (a
  server's `TargetTooFar` too). Not changed.

**A slip of mine.** One breakage list was written with a heredoc, against the note of the
day before. It worked, because nothing in it was a doubled backslash; the note stands.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **The socket is the default.** It is where the plan goes, the whole run makes the same
  calls of the server either way, a socket that cannot be had falls back to the routes
  and the event stream by itself, and one line in a browser's console goes back for good.
  What has no setting to undo it, the taking away of the routes' HTTP carriage, is still
  the operator's to see first.
- **The static data is kept in the transport**, as the other kept things are, and not in
  the page: the page still asks its one wallet route. When the wallet's calls are the
  page's own to make (Phase 6b), the keeping moves with them.

## 2026-10-10 — Phase 6b begun: the page makes the wallet's calls itself, as the client's services make them

Commits `2764849` and `ddea0f2`, pushed. Next's head: Phase 6b begun, with the wallet.

**What a retail client does** (the recordings first, then its code).

- On Tranquility ("Open Wallet - Plex - Corp Wallet - Corp Transfers") a wallet opened is:
  `account.GetCashBalance(1, accountKey=None)` (the corporation's wealth, for a pilot who
  may see it), the loyalty points and the bills, `account.GetTransactions(1000, None, None,
  False)`, the names of who is in them, and `account.GetEntryTypes()` once. The pilot's own
  balance is not asked: it was had at the login.
- `walletSvc.py` 41: the wallet service asks `GetCashBalance(0)` once as it starts, and keeps
  it. `accountsvc.py`: the transactions kept by month until the server says the account
  changed (108, 64); the entry kinds asked once and kept (86); the divisions kept five
  minutes (132).
- `bco_corporations.py` 138, `GetDivisionNames`: a hangar division is named by the
  corporation's `division1` to `division7`; a wallet division by `walletDivision2` to
  `walletDivision7`, and the first by no column, since it is the master wallet and has
  the client's own word.

**What was built.**

- **The wallet's asking, written once** (`web/src/bridge/walletReads.ts`). The page asked one
  route of the BFF and the route made five calls. A retail client has no such route: its
  services make the calls. That asking is now TypeScript the page and the hosted bots
  share, each call made by the generic call (`POST /api/bridge/call`) and so carried on
  the pilot's socket; the BFF relays it.

      account.GetCashBalance(0)
      account.GetTransactions(1000, None, None, False)
      account.GetEntryTypes()                 asked once and kept, until the pilot is another
      account.GetWalletDivisionsInfo()
      corpRegistry.GetCorporation()           for the wallet divisions' names

- **The asking itself** (`bridgeAsk`, `web/src/app/api.ts`): one call with a flow's own token,
  fetch and guard, and the notifications that came with its answer handed on as a route's
  answer's are.
- **A bot's wallet watch asks for the pilot's ISK alone.** It read the whole wallet, five
  calls, for one number.
- **The route still stands** (`GET /api/bridge/wallet`). Nothing of the page's asks it.

**A fault found by reading the client for it.** The corporation's row has `division1` to
`division7` and `walletDivision1` to `walletDivision7`. The route named the wallet's
divisions by the first seven, which are the hangar's, and so the page had. Both now name
them as the client does. On this server the two sets are "Division N" and "Wallet
Division N", so the Corp Wallet said "Division 2" where the corporation says "Wallet
Division 2".

**Proof.**

- 8 new tests and 7 answered anew: six of the asking (the calls and how each is asked; the
  kinds asked once, by three at once, after another pilot, after a failure, and with a
  late failure from before; each read failing by itself; a session lost; the ISK alone;
  the names), one of the route's names, one of `bridgeAsk`. The flow's seven wallet tests
  describe the same wallets as before and are answered call by call.
- 28 ways of breaking it were tried, four of a file at a time. One survived at first (an
  old asking that fails late taking away what was asked for since) and has a test now.
- With the sources of the commit before: 7 fail. Suite: 10173 tests, 10149 pass, 0 fail,
  0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **Side by side, live, on both transports.** For pilots of three corporations (one with a
  corporation's wallet to read), the route was asked and then the page's own asking made
  through the generic call, and the two answers compared whole.

  | | the game port | the gateway |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | Test Two, GM Elysian, Farmer, before the names were mended | the same, all three | the same but for the entry kinds |
  | Test Two, Farmer, after | the same, both | the same but for the entry kinds |
  | the second read of the page's | four calls: the kinds were kept | four calls |

  Through the gateway the entry kinds come wrapped as the server's cached answer, with
  the time it was made: one leaf of 322 differs, and differs as much between one call and
  the next as between the route and the page.
- **In the browser** (the default, the game port; Test Two): the Wallet window with its
  balance and its activity, the Corp Wallet saying the corporation has no divisions. The
  route was asked by nothing: none on the socket, none over HTTP. The five calls went as
  frames of the generic call: three of each of four, the page reading the wallet three
  times at a login, and the kinds once. A login is 86 frames where it was 83 or 84. The
  game port's ledger has all five as the client's own calls.
- The BFF's log: no error. The gateway's tally: nothing of a pilot's. The page was left
  with nobody in; the store was put back and the copy deleted.

**Measured and left.**

- **The page reads the whole wallet three times at a login**, once for each of three windows
  that want it. A client asks for the balance once and keeps it, moved by the server's
  word (`OnAccountChange`), asks for the transactions when the wallet's window opens and
  keeps them until that word, and asks for the divisions only for a pilot who may see the
  corporation's wallet. That is the next step of this: the keeping.
- **The first wallet division, and one with no name, say "Division N" on the page.** The
  client says its own words ("the master wallet", and a default for each). They are the
  install's, to be had as the page has its other words; not copied here.
- **A corporation's wallet with divisions was not seen in the browser**: the pilots in this
  browser's hangar are in corporations with none to show. It was read by the script.
- **The hangar's row for a pilot said where it was last seen**, a docking that the store's
  being put back had undone, until the pilot was next logged in. Of my own making.
- **What else a client asks as its wallet opens** (the loyalty points, the bills, the
  corporation's wealth by `GetCashBalance(1, …)`) was not set beside what the page asks.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **The first feature moved is the wallet, whole.** Its route was five reads and no write,
  which is the smallest whole thing a route does. A write's route also checks and
  confirms; that pattern is to be worked out on one small write before many are moved.
- **The route is left standing**, as the plan says of the routes until their HTTP carriage
  is taken away with the operator's word. It was mended where it was wrong.
- **What a call's answer brings with it is handed on.** The route's answer brought none of
  the notifications its five calls drained. The page's own calls hand theirs to the flow,
  as every other route's answer does.

## 2026-10-10 — the wallet kept as the client keeps it, and its balance moved by the server's word

Commit `1d27f12`, pushed. Next's head: the wallet kept as the client keeps it.

**What a retail client does** (the recordings first, then its code).

- The server's word that an account changed is `OnAccountChange(accountKey, ownerID,
  balance)`. On Tranquility ("Open Wallet - Plex - Corp Wallet - Corp Transfers") one
  transfer was two of them: `('cash', <the character>, 922932000.0)` to the client, and
  `('cash', <its corporation>, 935199.43)` to the corporation's members who may see that
  account. The key is the account's name, not its number.
- `walletSvc.py` 80: for the pilot's own (`'cash'` and the session's character) the balance
  kept is the one the server says, with nothing asked; for one of the corporation's seven
  (`'cash'` to `'cash7'` and the session's corporation) the division's balance is. A balance
  of nothing is left alone.
- `accountsvc.py` 64: at any such word the transactions kept are let go, and asked for when
  next wanted. 132: the divisions are good for five minutes.
- This server sends it from the one place its wallets are changed
  (`services/account/walletState.js`, `services/corporation/corpWalletState.js`), with the
  same three things.

**What was wrong.** The page read the whole wallet for each window that wanted it, three
at a login, and did not listen for `OnAccountChange` at all: a balance on show stayed as
it was until the window was read again.

**What was built** (`web/src/bridge/walletReads.ts`, and the flow's hearing of the two
notices).

- The pilot's ISK is asked for once and kept; `OnAccountChange('cash', the pilot, balance)`
  makes it that balance, with nothing asked.
- The transactions are kept until any `OnAccountChange`.
- The corporation's divisions are kept five minutes, and let go when one of its seven
  accounts changes (the client works the new balance in; this asks again, which is sooner
  and never behind). Its row is kept until `OnCorporationChanged`.
- Several windows that want the wallet together wait for the one asking of each thing.
- A wallet that has been read is drawn again when the server says an account changed:
  from what is kept, asking only for the transactions.
- The window's own Refresh asks the server afresh for all but the entry kinds. A bot's
  wallet watch asks the server each time, as before: it is a guard, and not a window.

**Proof.**

- 5 new tests of the keeping (one of them in place of an earlier one, which it says more
  than) and one of the flow hearing the notices; two of the earlier ones say more. 32 ways
  of breaking it were tried, four of a file at a time: all caught (a thirty-third in my
  list broke nothing, an unused name).
- With the sources of the commit before, 8 fail. Suite: 10178 tests, 10154 pass, 0 fail,
  0 cancelled, 24 skipped.
- **In the browser** (the default, the game port; Test Two docked, its Wallet and Corp Wallet
  windows open):

  | | before (`2764849`) | now |
  | --- | --- | --- |
  | the pilot's ISK asked for at a login | 3 times | once |
  | the transactions, the divisions, the corporation's row | 3 times each | once each |
  | the entry kinds | once | once |

  Then, with the wallet on show, Test Pilot (another account) gave Test Two 250 ISK through
  the BFF's own route. The server pushed `OnAccountChange ["cash", 140000002, 9999207668]`.
  The window said 9,999,207,668 ISK where it had said 9,999,207,418, with a new first
  entry, "Player Donation +250 ISK", and nobody pressed anything. Asked of the server
  since the login: the transactions, once. The balance: not at all.
- The window's Refresh then asked for the balance, the transactions, the divisions and
  the corporation's row once each, and not the kinds.
- The BFF's log: no error. The gateway's tally: nothing of a pilot's. The page was left
  with nobody in; the store was put back, which undid the gift, and the copy deleted.

**Not done.**

- **The corporation's side was not seen live.** No pilot in this browser's hangar is in a
  corporation whose wallet it may see. What a division's account changing does is in the
  tests.
- **The page asks for the divisions whoever the pilot is.** The client asks only for a pilot
  who may see its corporation's wallet (`HaveAccessToCorpWallet`: its roles), and the page
  is told none of the session's roles.
- **The master wallet's own word, and a nameless division's**, are still "Division N".
- **Through the gateway** the pushes come by the same stream and were not run live for this.

**Decisions taken in the operator's place.**

- **Refresh still asks the server.** The client has no such button and needs none. The
  page has one, and a button that asked nothing would be a lie.
- **A bot's watch is not answered from what is kept.** If the server ever failed to say an
  account had changed, a window would be a little out of date; a watch that guards a
  bot's spending would be wrong for the whole run.
- **A gift of ISK between two test pilots was made live** by a route whose own note says it
  had never been fired. It is the test server's ISK, 250 of it, and the store was put back.
